In [1]:
## Setup!
import math
<h1 id="Review-Questions:-Periodic-Motion">Review Questions: Periodic Motion¶</h1>
  1. Which statement best defines simple harmonic motion?
<p>"B. The restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and opposite to it.". Recall Hooke's Law, which is the definition of Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM).</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} F &= -k x \\ a &= -\omega^2 x \end{align} $$</p>
  1. An oscillator completes $n = 12 \; \text{full cycles}$ in $t = 3.0 \; \text{s}$. What are its frequency $f$, period $t$, and angular frequency $\omega$?
<p>Recall that frequency is the number of cycles per second. So it can be represented by the following formula:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} f &= \frac{n}{t} \\ &= \frac{12}{3.0 \; \text{s}} \\ &= 4.0 \; \text{Hz} \end{align} $$</p>
In [2]:
n = 12.0 ## full cycles
t =  3.0 ## s
f = n / t ## 1 / s = Hz
print(f"n = {n} full cycles\n"
      f"t = {t:.14g} s\n"
      f"f = {f} Hz")

n = 12.0 full cycles
t = 3 s
f = 4.0 Hz
<p>We can then compute for period $T$ as it is the reciprocal of frequency $f$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} T &= \frac{1}{f} \\ &= \frac{1}{4.0 \; \text{Hz}} \\ &= 0.25 \; \text{s} \end{align} $$</p>
In [3]:
T = 1 / f
print(f"T = {T} s")

T = 0.25 s
<p>Lastly, the angular frequency $\omega$ can be derived from another formula for frequency $f$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} ( f &= \frac{\omega}{2 \pi} ) \frac{2 \pi}{1} \\ \omega &= 2 \pi f \\ &= 2 \pi * 4.0 \; \text{Hz} \\ &= 2 \pi * 4.0 \; \frac{1}{\text{s}} \\ &= 8 \pi \frac{1}{\text{s}} \\ &= 25.13 \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}} \end{align} $$</p>
In [4]:
## 2 * math.pi == math.tau
print(f"math.pi * 2 = {math.pi * 2:.14g}\n"
      f"math.tau    = {math.tau:.14g}")

omega = math.tau * f
print(f"omega = {omega} rad / s")

math.pi * 2 = 6.2831853071796
math.tau    = 6.2831853071796
omega = 25.132741228718345 rad / s
  1. The amplitude $A$ of a mass-spring oscillator is doubled (with the same mass $m$ and spring constant $k$). What happens to the period $T$, maximum speed $v_{max}$, and total energy $E$?
<p>Recall that in the section Energy in SHM, the period $T$ is independent of the amplitude $A$.</p> <p>Let $A' = 2A$. Since $v_{max} = \omega A' = \omega 2A$, it doubles. Since $E = \frac{1}{2} k \times A'^2 = \frac{1}{2} k \times 2A'^2$, its exponential nature means a doubling of the amplitude $A$ results in a quadrupling of the total energy $E$.</p> <p><img alt="image.png" /></p> <p>Proof that $v_{max} = \omega A$ when $x = 0$:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} x(t) &= A \cos{(\omega t + \phi)} \\ \dfrac{0}{A} &= \dfrac{A \cos{(\omega t + \phi)}}{A} \\ 0 &= \cos{(\omega t + \phi)} \end{align} $$</p>
  1. A glider on a spring is momentarily at $x = -A$. Which description is correct?
<p>The maximum amplitude $A$ is at either extreme. In this case, the negative extreme (i.e. $-A$) is the leftmost. At this point, the glider has a speed $v_x = 0$ because it is about to switch directions. However, no matter the extreme, the restoring force always points toward equilibrium.</p>
  1. Several tuning forks have tines of different mass. Which produces the lowest pitch?
<p>Recall the formula for frequency, given some mass $m$:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} f = \frac{1}{2} \pi \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \end{align} $$</p> <p>Because the mass $m$ is in the denominator, this means that mass is indirectly proportional to the resulting frequency $f$. Thus larger masses result in lower frequencies, assuming the same spring constant $k$.</p>
  1. For $x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$, which phase angle $\phi$ describes an object that is at $x = 0$ and $t = 0$ and moving in the $+x$ direction?
<p>Recall the formula for displacement as a function of time for simple harmonic motion, substituting in displacement $x = 0 \; \text{m}$ and time $t = 0 \; \text{s}$. We are effectively looking for the phase angle at the starting point of the graph.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} x(t) &= A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \\ 0 &= A \cos(\omega \times 0 + \phi) \\ 0 &= A \cos(\phi) \\ \text{since:} \\ \cos(0) &= 1 \\ \text{thus:} \\ 0 &= A \cos(0) \\ 0 &= A \times 1 \\ 0 &= A \\ \text{thus:} \\ \phi &= 0 \end{align} $$</p>
  1. A particle's position is $x(t) = (0.30 \; \text{m}) \cos(4 \pi t + \frac{\pi}{3})$, with $t$ in seconds. What are its period $T$ and maximum speed $v_{max}$?
<p>So we are to use the equation for Position $x$ as a function of time $t$, with the following givens:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} x(t) &= (0.30 \; \text{m}) \cos(4 \pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}) \\ A &= 0.30 \; \text{m} \\ \omega &= 4 \pi \; \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}} \\ t &= \; ? \; \text{s} \\ \phi &= \frac{\pi}{3} \; \text{rad} \end{align} $$</p>
In [5]:
A     = 0.30 ## m
omega = 4 * math.pi ## rad / s
phi   = math.pi / 3 ## rad

print(f"A = {A}\nomega = {omega}\nphi = {phi}")

A = 0.3
omega = 12.566370614359172
phi = 1.0471975511965976
<p>Since we have $\omega$, we can determine the frequency $f$:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} f &= \frac{\omega \; \dfrac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}}}{2 \pi} \\ &= \frac{4 \pi \; \dfrac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}}}{2 \pi} \\ &= 2 \; \frac{1}{\text{s}} \\ &= 2 \; \text{Hz} \end{align} $$</p> <p>With the frequency $f$, we can determine the period $T$:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} T &= \frac{1}{f} \\ &= \frac{1}{2 \; \text{Hz}} \\ &= \frac{1}{2 \; \dfrac{1}{\text{s}}} \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \dfrac{\text{s}}{1} \\ &= 0.5 \; \text{s} \end{align} $$</p> <p>The determine the velocity, we need to use the graph of displacement and velocity for simple harmonic motion. The graph states that $v_{max} = \omega A$. So:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} v_{max} &= \omega A \\ &= 4 \pi \; \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}} \times 0.30 \; \text{m} \\ &= 3.77 \; \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \end{align} $$</p>
In [6]:
v_max = omega * A
print(f"v_max = {v_max}")

v_max = 3.7699111843077517
  1. A block with mass $m = 0.200 \; \text{kg}$, on a horizontal spring, with spring constant $k = 80.0 \; \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}$ oscillates with an amplitude $A = 0.100 \; \text{m}$. What are its maximum speed and maximum acceleration?
<p>Recall the formulas used for Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion. Recall that $v_{max}$ occurs as displacement $x = 0$. Let's derive the formula for some speed $v_x$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} E &= \dfrac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 \\ \text{thus:} \\ ( \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 ) - (\dfrac{1}{2} k x^2) \\ ( \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 ) \times \dfrac{2}{m} \\ \dfrac{2}{m} \times \dfrac{1}{2} k ( A^2 - x^2 ) &= {v_x}^2 \\ {v_x}^2 &= \dfrac{k}{m} (A^2 - x^2) \\ \sqrt{{v_x}^2} &= \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m} (A^2 - x^2)} \\ v_x &= \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} \times \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} \end{align} $$</p>
<p>Now let's use the formula for some speed $v_x$, where $x = 0$ because that is where $v_{max}$ occurs:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} v_x &= \; \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \times \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} \\ &= \; \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \times \sqrt{A^2 - 0^2} \\ &= \; \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \times \sqrt{A^2} \\ &= \; \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \times A \\ \text{where:} \\ \omega &= \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \\ \text{thus:} \\ v_{max} &= \omega A \end{align} $$</p> <p>So we can solve for the angular frequency $\omega$ first and then multiply it to the amplitude $A$ to get the maximum speed $v_{max}$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align*} \omega &= \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{80.0 \; \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} }{0.200 \; \text{kg}} } \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{80.0 \; \dfrac{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} \cdot \text{s}^{-2}} {\text{m}} }{0.200 \; \text{kg}} } \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{80.0 \; \text{s}^{-2} }{0.200} } = \sqrt{\frac{80.0 \; \dfrac{1}{\text{s}^2} }{0.200} } \\ &= \sqrt{400 \; \frac{1}{\text{s}^2}} \\ &= 20 \; \frac{1}{\text{s}} = 20 \; \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}} \end{align*} $$</p> <p>Then:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align*} v_x &= \omega A \\ &= 20 \; \frac{1}{\text{s}} \times 0.100 \; \text{m} \\ &= 2.0 \; \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \end{align*} $$</p> <p>So the maximum speed is $v_{max} = 2.0 \; \dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$. To get the maximum acceleration $a_{max}$, we can use the following formula:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align*} a_{max} &= - \frac{k}{m} (-A) \\ &= - \frac{80.0 \; \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} }{0.200 \; \text{kg}} (- 0.100 \; \text{m}) \\ &= - \frac{80.0 \; \text{kg} \cdot \text{m} \cdot \text{s}^{-2} \times \dfrac{1}{\text{m}} }{0.200 \; \text{kg}} (- 0.100 \; \text{m}) \\ &= - \frac{80.0 \; \text{s}^{-2} }{0.200} \; (- 0.100 \; \text{m}) \\ &= 40 \; \text{m} \cdot \text{s}^{-2} \\ &= 40 \; \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} \end{align*} $$</p>

alt="image.png" /></p>
  1. A block with mass $m = 0.50 \; \text{kg}$ on a spring oscillates at frequency $f = 2.0 \; \text{Hz}$. If it is replaced by another block with new mass $m' = 2.0 \; \text{kg}$ on the same spring, what is the new frequency?
<p>First, we need to somehow relate mass and frequency. Recall that for an angular frequency $\omega$:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} \omega &= \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \\ f &= \frac{\omega}{2 \pi} = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \times \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \\ T &= \frac{1}{f} = \frac{2 \pi}{\omega} \end{align} $$</p>
<p>The relation $T = \frac{1}{f}$ is useful because we can directly solve for the time period $T$ and relate it back to get the angular frequency $\omega$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} T &= \frac{1}{f} \\ &= \frac{1}{2.0 \; \cfrac{1}{\text{s}}} = \frac{1}{2.0} \; \text{s} \\ &= 0.5 \; \text{s} \\ \text{thus:} \\ T &= \frac{2 \pi}{\omega} \\ T \times \dfrac{\omega}{1} &= \frac{2 \pi}{\omega} \times \dfrac{\omega}{1} \\ \dfrac{T \omega}{T} &= \dfrac{2 \pi}{T} \\ \omega &= \dfrac{2 \pi}{T} \\ \text{thus:} \\ \omega &= \frac{2 \pi}{0.5 \; \text{s}} \\ &= 12.57 \; \frac{1}{\text{s}} = 12.57 \; \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}} \end{align} $$</p>
In [8]:
f = 2.0 ## Hz
T = 1.0 / f ## s
omega = math.tau / T ## rad / s

print(f"f = {f} Hz\nT = {T} s\nomega = {omega} rad / s")

f = 2.0 Hz
T = 0.5 s
omega = 12.566370614359172 rad / s
<p>We can then use the angular frequency $f$ to calculate the spring force constant $k$. The $k$ for the initial block should be the same as the $k$ for the second one.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} \omega &= \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \\ \omega &= \dfrac{\sqrt{k}}{\sqrt{m}} \\ \omega \times \dfrac{\sqrt{m}}{1} &= \dfrac{\sqrt{k}}{\sqrt{m}} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{m}}{1} \\ \omega \sqrt{m} &= \sqrt{k} \\ (\sqrt{k})^2 &= (\omega \sqrt{m})^2 \\ k &= \omega^2 m \\ \text{thus:} \\ k &= (12.57 \; \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}})^2 \times 0.50 \; \text{kg} \\ k &= 157.0049 \; \frac{1}{\text{s}^2} \times 0.50 \; \text{kg} \\ k &= 79 \; \text{kg} \cdot \text{s}^{-2} \end{align} $$</p>
In [9]:
m = 0.50 ## kg
k = omega**2 * m ## kg / s^2

print(f"{omega**2} rad^2 / s^2")
print(f"m = {m} kg\nk = {k} kg / s^2")

157.91367041742973 rad^2 / s^2
m = 0.5 kg
k = 78.95683520871486 kg / s^2
<p>We can now solve for the new frequency $f'$ when a block with some other mass $m' = 2.0 \; \text{kg}$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} f' &= \frac{1}{2 \pi} \times \sqrt{\frac{k}{m'}} \\ &= \frac{1}{2 \pi} \times \sqrt{\frac{79 \; \text{kg} \cdot \text{m} \cdot \text{s}^{-2}} {2.0 \; \text{kg}} } \\ &= \frac{1}{2 \pi} \times \sqrt{39.5 \; \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}} \\ &= 1 \; \text{Hz} \end{align} $$</p>

  1. A mass-spring system has amplitude $A$. When the mass is at displacement $x = \dfrac{A}{2}$ what fraction of the total energy is kinetic?
<p>Recall the section Energy in SHM.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} E &= K + U \\ (-U) + E &= K + U + (-U) \\ K &= E - U \\ \text{where:} \\ E &= \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 \\ K &= \dfrac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 \\ U &= \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 \\ \text{thus:} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 \\ \text{where:} \\ x &= \dfrac{A}{2} \\ \text{thus:} \\ K &= E - U \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} k \frac{A^2}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} k (A^2 - \dfrac{A^2}{4}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} k ( A^2 \dfrac{4}{4} - \dfrac{A^2}{4}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} k (\dfrac{4A^2 - A^2}{4}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} k (\dfrac{3A^2}{4}) \\ \end{align} $$</p> <p>Thus the factor for kinetic energy $K$ is $\dfrac{3}{4}$. Note that we don't consider the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ as part of the factor because that's part of the equation.</p>
  1. A spring with mass $m = 0.250 \; \text{kg}$ has mass constant $k = 100 \; \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}$ and amplitude $A = 0.20 \; \text{m}$. What is its speed $v_x$ when displacement $x = 0.12 \; \text{m}$?
<p>This is an application of the equation for Energy. We have all the parameters sans speed $v_x$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} E &= K + U \\ K &= E - U \\ \text{where:} \\ E &= \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 \\ K &= \dfrac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 \\ U &= \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 \\ \text{thus:} \\ K &= E - U \\ \dfrac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 \\ \dfrac{\cfrac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 }{\cfrac{1}{2} m} &= \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} k (A^2 - x^2) }{\cfrac{1}{2} m} \\ {v_x}^2 &= \dfrac{k (A^2 - x^2)}{m} \\ \sqrt{{v_x}^2} &= \sqrt{\dfrac{k (A^2 - x^2)}{m}} \\ v_x &= \sqrt{\dfrac{k (A^2 - x^2)}{m}} \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{100 \; \cfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} \times \left[(0.20 \; \text{m})^2 - (0.12 \; \text{m})^2 \right] }{0.250 \; \text{kg}} } \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{100 \; \cfrac{kg \cdot m \cdot s^{-2} }{\text{m}} \times (0.04 \; \text{m}^2 - 0.0144 \; \text{m}^2) }{0.250 \; \text{kg}} } \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{100 \; s^{-2} \times 0.0256 \; \text{m}^2 }{0.250} } \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{2.56 \; \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2} }{0.250} } \\ &= \sqrt{10.42 \; \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2}} \\ &= 3.2 \; \text{m} \cdot \text{s}^{-1} = 3.2 \; \dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \end{align} $$</p>

  1. A spring has spring force constant $k = 200 \;\frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}$ and oscillates with amplitude $A = 0.050 \; \text{m}$. What is the kinetic energy at displacement $x = 0.030 \; \text{m}$?
<p>The techanical energy $E$ is composed of kinetic energy $K$ and potential energy $U$. They are given by the following formulas:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} E &= K + U \\ (-U) + E &= K + U + (-U) \\ K &= E - U \\ \text{where:} \\ E &= \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 \\ K &= \frac{1}{2} m {v_x}^2 \\ U &= \frac{1}{2} k x^2 \\ \text{thus:} \\ K &= \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} k (A^2 - x^2) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 200 \; \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} \times \left[(0.050\; \text{m})^2 - (0.030 \; \text{m})^2\right] \\ &= 100 \; \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} \times \left[0.0025 \; \text{m}^2 - 0.0009 \; \text{m}^2 \right] \\ &= 100 \; \dfrac{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} \cdot \text{s}^{-2}}{\text{m}} \times (0.0016 \; \text{m}^2) \\ &= 100 \; \text{kg} \cdot \text{s}^{-2} \times 0.0016 \; \text{m}^2 \\ &= 0.16 \; \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2} \\ &= 0.16 \; \text{kg} \cdot \dfrac{\text{m}^2}{\text{s}^2} = 0.16 \; \text{J} \end{align} $$</p> <p>Thus, at displacment $x = 0.030 \; \text{m}$, the kinetic energy is $K = 0.16 \; \text{J}$.</p>

  1. A mass $m = 0.40 \; \text{kg}$ hung on a vertical spring is stretched $L = 0.098 \; \text{m}$ to reach equilibrium. If the mass is pulled down slightly and released, what is the period of oscillation?
<p>This is a Vertical SHM problem. To predict the period of oscillation $t$, we first need the spring force constant $k$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} k &= \frac{m g}{L} \\ &= \frac{0.40 \; \text{kg} \times 9.81 \; \cfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} }{0.098 \; \text{m}} \\ &= 4.0 \; \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{s}^2} \end{align} $$</p>

<p>With the spring force constant $k$, we can predict the period of oscillation $t$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} \omega &= \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{0.098 \; \cfrac{\text{kg}}{\text{s}^2} }{0.40 \; \text{kg}} } \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{0.098 \; \cfrac{1}{\text{s}^2} }{0.40} } \\ &= \sqrt{100.102 \; \cfrac{1}{\text{s}^2}} \\ &= 10.01 \; \dfrac{1}{\text{s}} = 10.01 \; \dfrac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}} \\ \text{thus:} \\ \omega &= 2 \pi f \\ f &= \dfrac{\omega}{2 \pi} \\ &= \dfrac{10.01 \; \dfrac{\text{rad} }{\text{s}} }{2 \pi} \\ &= 1.59 \; \text{Hz} \\ \text{thus:} \\ T &= \frac{1}{f} \\ &= \frac{1}{1.59 \; \text{Hz}} \\ &= 0.628 \; \text{s} \end{align} $$</p>

  1. A watch's balance wheel has moment of intertia $I = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \; \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2$ and its spring has torsion constant $\kappa = 8.0 \times 10^{-4} \; \text{N} \cdot \dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{rad}}$. What is the period of oscillation?
<p>This is an Angular SHM problem, specifically dealing with torsional oscillators. Recall that this is the rotational analog of Hooke's law, i.e. $F_x = -k x$, where it instead produces angular simple harmonic motion. Every SHM formula from Key Equations of SHM has a rotational counterpart, so you just swap out the following:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} \text{Displacement } x &\rightarrow \text{Angle } \theta \\ \text{Mass } m &\rightarrow \text{Moment of Inertia } I \\ \text{Spring force constant } k &\rightarrow \text{Torsion constant } \kappa \end{align} $$</p>
<p>In this question, since we have $k = \kappa$ and $m = I$, we can calculate the period of oscillation $T$ in terms of the angular frequency $\omega$.</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} \omega &= \sqrt{\dfrac{\text{k}}{\text{m}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\kappa}{I}} \\ \omega &= 2 \pi f \\ f &= \frac{\omega}{2 \pi} \\ \text{since:} \\ T &= \frac{1}{f} \\ \text{thus:} \\ T &= \frac{1}{\cfrac{\omega}{2 \pi}} \\ &= \frac{2 \pi}{\omega} \\ &= \frac{2 \pi }{\sqrt{\cfrac{\kappa}{I}} } \\ &= \frac{2 \pi }{\cfrac{\sqrt{\kappa}}{\sqrt{I}} } \\ &= \frac{2 \pi \sqrt{I} }{\sqrt{\kappa} } \\ &= \frac{2 \pi \sqrt{2.0 \times 10^{-6} \; \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2} }{\sqrt{8.0 \times 10^{-4} \; \text{kg} \cdot \text{m} \cdot \text{s}^{-2} \cdot \cfrac{ \text{m} }{ \text{rad} } } } \\ &= 0.314 \; \text{s} \end{align} $$</p>

<p>Recall the formula for the period $T$ of a simple pendulum:</p> <p>$$\begin{align} T &= 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \end{align}$$</p> <p>Since neither mass $m$ nor swing angle $theta$ are involved in the formula, the period remains unchanged.</p>
  1. What length must a simple pendulum have to give a period of $t = 3.00 \; \text{s}$?
<p>We can use the formula for the period $T$ of a simple pendulum to isolate the length $L$. $$ \begin{align} T &= 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \\ T &= 2 \pi \frac{\sqrt{L}}{\sqrt{g}} \\ \frac{\sqrt{g}}{2 \pi} \times T &= \sqrt{L}\\ L &= (T \frac{\sqrt{g}}{2 \pi})^2 \\ &= T^2 \frac{g}{4 \pi^2} \\ &= (3.00 \; \text{s})^2 \times \frac{9.81 \; \cfrac{\text{m} }{\text{s}^2} }{4 \pi^2} \\ &= 9.00 \; \text{s}^2 \times 0.2485 \; \dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} \\ &= 2.23 \; \text{m} \end{align} $$</p>

<p>Recall the formua for the period $T$ of a simple pendulum:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} T &= 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \\ T &= 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{6 g}} \\ \end{align} $$</p> <p>Since $g$ is inversely proportional to the period $T$, the period is decreased by a factor of the square root of the multiplier, i.e. $\sqrt{6}$.</p>

<p>Recall that the moment of inertia $I$ is an analog to mass $m$ in simple harmonic motion. Since we have that, we can use it to calculate</p> <p>$$ \begin{align} T &= 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \end{align} $$</p>

  1. A damped oscillator has a mass $m = 0.50 \; \text{kg}$ and damping constant $b = 0.10 \; \dfrac{\text{kg}}{\text{s}}$. Its amplitude envelope $A_e = A e^{-b t / 2m}$. How long does it take for the amplitude to fall to $1 / e$ of its initial value?
<p>$$ \begin{align} A_e &= A e^{-(b / 2 m) t} \\ \frac{\cfrac{1}{e}}{A} &= \frac{A e^{-bt/2m}}{A} \\ \frac{A}{e} &= e^{-bt/2m} \\ \text{where:} \\ b^y &= x \rightarrow log_b(x) = y \\ \text{thus:} \\ e^{-bt/2m} &= \frac{A}{e} \\ \log_e(\frac{A}{e}) &= -\frac{bt}{2m} \\ \log_e(A) - log_e(e) &= -\frac{bt}{2m} \\ \log_e(A) - 1 &= -\frac{bt}{2m} \\ \log_e{\frac{1}{e}} - 1 &= -\frac{bt}{2m} \\ \log_e(1) - \log_e{e} - 1 &= -\frac{bt}{2m} \\ 0 - 1 - 1 &= -\frac{bt}{2m} \\ -2 &= -\frac{bt}{2m} \\ -\frac{2m}{b} \times -2 &= -\frac{bt}{2m} \times -\frac{2m}{b} \\ t &= \frac{4m}{b} \end{align} $$</p>
